clauses.text: 134 TWENTY-FOURTH REPORT OF CIVIL SERVICE COMMISSION. through competitive examination or by transfer or promotion from a competi- tive position shall be transferred to a competitive position, Lieutenant-Colonel Hodges, of the Isthmian Canal Commission, requested Mr. Purvis's transfer, and in view of his three years' satisfactory service and his ill health due to service on the Isthmus the Commission recommended the issuance of the order. February 22, 1908. Mr. Edward J. Tupper may be appointed deputy collector and inspector of customs at Stamford, Conn., without compliance with the civil-service rules or the Executive order of January 17, 1873. The Treasury Department stated that this position pays the nominal salary of only $700 per annum, with no possible promotion ; that it i* necessary for the proper performance of the duties that the officer should reside in Stam- ford; that the eligible register for the district contained the names of three persons, each of whom received a higher salary in his position than that paid in the position in question, and that there was no probability of any of them moving to Stamford to perform the duties required at the salary paid. The collector at Bridgeport, Conn., In whose district Stamford i» located, asked for the appointment of Mr. Tupper, who is a prominent business man of Stamford and mayor of the city. His business is located on the water front, and the prominent business men of the city requested his appointment. The Executive order of January 17, 1873, which is mentioned, prohibits a Federal officeholder from holding a municipal office at the same time. March 4, 1908. Mr. Charles L. Babcock may be appointed as an immigrant inspector for con- fidential duty in the Immigration Service in the Department of Commerce and Labor without examination under the civil-service rules. The Department of Commerce and Labor has found it necessary, in order to investigate satisfactorily conditions surrounding the enforcement of the law relating to immigration, to assign a competent and absolutely reliable officer to the work. Such work requires that the man performing it possess not only tact, judgment, and skill, but also an absolutely unimpeachable character and a wide knowledge of affairs and of human nature. The employee who had been assigned to this duty was transferred to a somewhat similar position under the Department of Justice, and Mr. Babcock was appointed temporarily to the position. The work could not be completed during the period for which Mr. Babcock was temporarily appointed, and upon presenting the facts to the Com- mission it recommended to the President the issuance of the above order. Mr. Babeock's duties are of a confidential nature, and the position is analogous to positions which are excepted under the civil-service rules in other Departments, such as si>ecial employees in the Treasury Department and certain pension examiners and special agents in the Interior Department. March 6, 1908. Mr. Philip W. Reinhard, jr., of New York, confidential clerk to the collector of customs at New York, may be transferred from the excepted to the com- petitive class because of his faithful service during the past nine years, it being desirable that he continue In the performance of the responsible duties, classified in character, which he has been performing. Mr. Reinhard was appointed paymaster In the New York custom-house on March 7, 1891), with compensation at the rate of $2,500 per annum, the jx)sltion at that time being excepted. On May 27, 1902, he was transferred to the posi- tion of confidential clerk at $2,500 per annum, which i>osition was at that time and still is excepted. At the time of his appointment on May 27, ltK)2, Mr. Rein- was placed in charge of the customs bureau at the United States i>ost -office,
